rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which design choices matter. The most informative first experiment is the simplest possible baseline: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 (config_001). This establishes a performance floor using a fast, reliable linear encoder and a single profile, with no aggregation or fusion complexity. It serves as the reference against which all subsequent experiments can be compared to isolate the marginal contribution of multiprofile, learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), the image modality, aggregation strategies, and fusion methods. Starting here minimizes the risk of a failed or confounded first run and maximizes the interpretability of every later comparison, making it the best use of the first budget slot under complete uncertainty.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), so evidence is extremely sparse. The most fundamental uncertainty in a multimodal cellular profiling study is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest test of this: it matches config_001 in profile setting (singleprofile) and overall simplicity (no aggregation, no fusion), changing only the modality from RNA to image. If image-only accuracy is close to or exceeds 48.5%, it confirms that image features are a viable signal source and justifies investing budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If it is substantially lower, we learn that RNA is the dominant modality and can focus subsequent experiments on RNA encoder/aggregation choices rather than fusion strategies. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the highest-level design axis (modality) before committing budget to more granular questions like encoder choice, aggregation, or fusion type.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, establishing RNA as the dominant signal, while config_010 (image-only, resnet50) achieves only 20.8%, indicating the image modality is currently a weak or uninformative source. This leaves the RNA-side design choices as the highest-leverage area to explore. Question: config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) directly tests whether moving from a single profile to multiple profiles with average-pool aggregation improves RNA classification, while holding the encoder (pca_n2000) constant. This isolates the profile/aggregation effect in a clean A/B comparison against config_001. Why this is the best next step: Under a tight budget, understanding whether multiprofile aggregation adds value over singleprofile is a prerequisite for interpreting all downstream multimodal and multiprofile configurations (configs 018-051). If multiprofile does not help the RNA baseline, many complex configurations can be deprioritized; if it does, we gain a strong prior for which aggregation strategies to pair with fusion. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty about a design axis that affects the majority of remaining configurations.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc / 0.573 F1, a substantial +10.6 pt gain over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). This strongly indicates that multiprofile aggregation is the key lever for RNA performance. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for the same encoder and profile setting. Question tested: config_003 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer while holding model_setting, profile_setting, and rna_encoder identical to config_002, cleanly isolating the aggregation effect. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) it is a single-variable comparison extending the strongest finding, (2) the answer directly determines which aggregation to carry into all subsequent multimodal experiments (configs 020/021, 026/027, etc.), (3) it is low-risk since RNA already performs well, and (4) under a limited budget, resolving the aggregation choice before adding modality complexity avoids confounding multiple design decisions simultaneously.

Evidence: config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.591, F1 0.573), substantially outperforming the single-profile baseline (config_001, 0.485) and the transformer aggregation (config_003, 0.519). Image-only models are very weak (0.208). The only RNA encoder tested is PCA (linear, 2000-dim). Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the RNA representation itself is a meaningful design lever, or whether the profile/aggregation choices dominate. Question: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable change from config_002, swapping the linear PCA encoder for a learned non-linear variational representation at 200 dimensions. This isolates the effect of RNA encoder while holding the best-known profile and aggregation fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: If scvi_n200 matches or beats PCA, it reveals that learned representations add value and justifies further encoder exploration (scgpt) and multimodal combinations. If it underperforms PCA, it strongly suggests the linear structure is sufficient, allowing us to rule out an entire family of configurations (005–009 and their multimodal counterparts) and redirect budget toward fusion or image-encoder questions. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core design axis with a single experiment.

Evidence: RNA-only models dominate (0.485–0.650) while image-only with ResNet50 is very weak (0.208). Within RNA, multiprofile+avgpool is the best profile/aggregation combo, and scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 by ~6% (0.650 vs 0.591) under identical settings. Uncertainty: We have not yet tested the third RNA encoder (scGPT) under the same favorable conditions, so we do not know whether scGPT could surpass scvi_n200 or whether scvi_n200 is already near the encoder ceiling. Question tested: config_008 (rna_only, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) isolates the encoder variable while holding profile and aggregation fixed, giving a direct scGPT-vs-scvi_n200 comparison. Why best next: The RNA encoder is the highest-leverage design choice given RNA's dominance; resolving it before investing in multimodal or image-encoder experiments prevents committing budget to a suboptimal base representation. A clean single-variable comparison also yields the most interpretable evidence for all downstream fusion decisions.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + multi-profile + avgpool (config_005, 0.650) is the clear current best, and with PCA-2000, avgpool beat transformer by ~7 points (0.591 vs 0.519). However, scvi_n200 produces a learned nonlinear latent representation, so the aggregation interaction may differ. Question: Does the avgpool-over-transformer advantage hold for scvi_n200, or does the richer learned representation benefit from transformer-based aggregation? This is a clean single-variable comparison (config_005 vs config_006, only aggregation changes). Why best next: It definitively resolves the aggregation choice for the top-performing encoder, which will inform every subsequent experiment (including multimodal fusion). If avgpool remains superior, we can lock in that design and focus remaining budget on the more impactful question of whether multimodal fusion adds value. If transformer surprisingly helps, it opens a new promising direction. Either outcome reduces uncertainty about a core architectural decision with minimal confounding.

Evidence: RNA-only models (0.48–0.65) vastly outperform image-only (0.21), and the best RNA config is scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool (0.650). The critical open question is whether adding the image modality via fusion can complement the strong RNA signal or will dilute it. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests that question with the simplest fusion (concat) and the same image encoder (resnet50) already characterized in isolation. If it beats 0.650, multimodal fusion is a promising direction and we can then explore better image encoders (ViT-L) and weighted fusion. If it underperforms, we learn that the weak image features (0.208 standalone) do not contribute useful complementary signal, saving budget from exploring the many multimodal variants. This single experiment resolves the highest-uncertainty design decision (modality combination) before committing budget to finer-grained fusion/encoder variations.

Evidence: config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) scored 0.632, which is notably below the RNA-only scvi_n200 baselines (config_005: 0.650, config_006: 0.653), suggesting that naive concat fusion of a weak image modality (image-only resnet50: 0.208) actively hurts performance. Question: Does weighted fusion, which can down-weight the weaker image branch, recover the RNA-only performance or even exceed it? config_031 is identical to config_030 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating fusion as the sole variable. Why this is the best next step: It is the cleanest single-variable comparison available to determine whether resnet50 image carries any salvageable signal in a multimodal setting. If weighted fusion still underperforms RNA-only, we can confidently deprioritize resnet50-based multimodal configs and redirect budget toward RNA-only refinement or a stronger image encoder (ViT-L). If it recovers to ~0.65+, it justifies further multimodal exploration with resnet50. This single experiment resolves a critical fork in the search strategy under limited budget.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_031 (multimodal, scVI_n200, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.678 acc. However, the image-only ResNet50 baseline was extremely weak (0.208), raising uncertainty about whether the image modality is contributing meaningful signal or merely adding noise that the weighted fusion partially compensates for. Question: config_037 isolates a single variable—upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L—while keeping the rest of the pipeline identical to config_031 (scVI_n200, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted). This directly tests whether a stronger visual representation unlocks additional signal from the image modality. Why this is the best next experiment: (1) It is a clean one-factor comparison against our current best, so any performance change can be attributed to image encoder quality. (2) The answer has high strategic value: if ViT-L substantially improves over ResNet50, the image modality is a genuine contributor and further multimodal exploration is warranted; if it does not, we can conclude the image channel is not informative and redirect budget toward RNA-side improvements. (3) It avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously (unlike config_039, which would also change aggregation), preserving interpretability under a tight budget.
